sphl_manual.title: SPHL OPERATIONS MANUAL — PAGE 12
sphl_manual.body:
SELF-PROPELLED HYPERBARIC LIFEBOAT — OCCUPANT NOTICE

This craft is a pressure vessel. If you are reading this, the decompression schedule is running. Do NOT open the hatch until the surface-pressure gauge reads zero. Decompression at saturation depth is fatal and cannot be reversed.

The schedule cannot be shortened. It cannot be paused. It runs its six days regardless of anything outside the hull.

Ration the water. Stay off the hatch. Watch the gauge.

— Meridian Deep Energy, Marine Safety Division

pressure_log.title: AUTOMATED PRESSURE LOG
pressure_log.body:
DECOMPRESSION SCHEDULE — DAY 6 OF 6

DAY 1 — 09.2 BAR. OCCUPANT UNRESPONSIVE. VITALS STABLE.
DAY 2 — 07.4 BAR. OCCUPANT UNRESPONSIVE. VITALS STABLE.
DAY 3 — 05.1 BAR. OCCUPANT INTERMITTENTLY CONSCIOUS. SEDATION MAINTAINED PER PROTOCOL.
DAY 4 — 03.3 BAR. HULL CONTACT EVENT. DRIFT ANCHOR DEPLOYED.
DAY 5 — 01.9 BAR. OCCUPANT RESTLESS. SPOKE. NO CREW RESPONSE LOGGED.
DAY 6 — 01.0 BAR. SURFACE PRESSURE IMMINENT.

NOTE: NO RESPONSE FROM FIELD TRAFFIC CONTROL ON ANY CHANNEL. DAYS 1 THROUGH 6.

crew_letter_1.title: UNSENT LETTER — BUNKHOUSE CABIN 2
crew_letter_1.body:
Marta —

Three weeks more and I'm done. I mean it this time, don't laugh.

Money's still good. Other things aren't. They cut the food order again, second time now, and when Bjorn asked the galley the reason the galley didn't have one. Whole pallets going back out on the boat. Tinned goods. Out, not in. Nobody can make it make sense for me.

Osk stood the night watch Tuesday and came in grey. Wouldn't say what. Osk doesn't come in grey.

Don't write any of this back, your mother reads your letters out loud. Kiss the boys. Tell Erik his fish is still the biggest anyone's landed out here. It isn't. Tell him.

Three weeks.

— Henrik

crew_letter_2.title: NOTE TAPED INSIDE A LOCKER — CABIN 5
crew_letter_2.body:
For whoever gets this bunk —

Heater rattles. Wedge a coin in the grate and it quits. Third rung on the aft ladder's gone soft, don't trust it with a full crate. Cook does real eggs on Sundays if you beat the pump crew to the line.

One more thing. Don't get the lads started on the rig at the far end of the chain. Not because there's trouble in it. Because there's no answer in it — you'll watch a grown man work out that he's got no idea where half his own supper goes, and then he's no use for cards the rest of the night.

Leave the coin for the next fella.

— G.

rationing_memo.title: OPERATIONS MEMO — GALLEY COPY, GREASE-STAINED
rationing_memo.body:
FROM: MERIDIAN DEEP ENERGY — LOGISTICS
TO: SALTLINE GALLEY STATIONS
RE: PROVISIONING ADJUSTMENT, EFFECTIVE THIS CYCLE

Standing resupply is reduced forty percent through quarter end. Implement portion scheduling per the attached table. Section leads will field crew questions. Section leads have not been told the reason and are not to speculate on it.

Under the print, in pen, gone over twice:
'40 percent to WHERE. we are 900 mile from land. nothing leaves this water but the supply boat and the boat only runs one way — down the line. so who is eating our food.'

quiet_rig_note.title: TALLY BOOK PAGE — REC ROOM, UNDER THE DARTBOARD
quiet_rig_note.body:
Werner's cousin crewed the supply run a season. Says the men on the end platform signed papers thick as your wrist and never once talked money. Says they offload out there at night with no hands on deck — crane does the whole job on its own, in the dark.

Kristjan put it to the company man flat at the safety brief. What do you call the last rig, then. Company man smiles. 'Processing terminus.' Processing what. Smiles again. Moves us along.

We call it the Quiet Rig now, between ourselves. Stupid name. It stuck anyway.

Werner still owes me a bottle off Thursday's board. Putting it in writing so he can't wriggle out.

breaker_notice.title: STATION NOTICE — MAIN POWER IS OFF
breaker_notice.body:
POSTED AT THE STAIR HEAD

Topside floodlights are DEAD. The master breaker for that circuit — 4-A — is thrown. An arc fault burned the feed line and it was that or a fire on the deck. Until someone brings it back the deck goes black at nightfall, and the deck is not safe black. You'll find out why.

To raise the lights, climb the stair tower off this deck:

  LEVEL 1 — MACHINERY / CABLE STORES. A spool of feed cable is racked here. TAKE IT.
  LEVEL 2 — BREAKER ROOM 4-A. Splice the burned gap with the spool FIRST. THEN close Master 4-A.

That order. Not the other way round, unless you fancy the flash. The maintenance log on the panel tells you the same.

Before dark. I mean it.

— last watch

breaker_log.title: MAINTENANCE LOG — BREAKER ROOM 4-A
breaker_log.body:
ELECTRICAL — RUNNING LOG

04 — Topside flood circuit tripping under load. Feed line in the stairwell run's corroded, that's my money. Flagged for splice.

09 — Splice held up. Requisition for spool cable came back DENIED. Every reel off my inventory 'redirected down the line.' Second time this month something I need goes down the line and doesn't come back up it.

11 — Scorch on the corridor run. Arc fault. Killed the whole circuit at the master before it took the corridor with it. Topside stays dark till I get cable, and I'll not be getting cable.

Whoever comes after me: splice the corridor gap FIRST, THEN throw the master here. That order. Get it backwards and you'll wear your own face on the panel.

— E.V.

machine_shop_sign.title: NOTICE — MACHINE SHOP WINDOW
machine_shop_sign.body:
MACHINE SHOP SEALED — BY ORDER OF THE OIM

Hot-work permits pulled pending inquiry into unauthorized fabrication.

Under the notice, scratched into the paint with something sharp:

'they know about the raft.'

lookout_note.title: WEATHERED NOTEBOOK — LOOKOUT POINT
lookout_note.body:
Nobody comes up the mast but me and the birds, which suits me.

Clear day, you can count all seven from up here. Ours, then the rest of them east, smaller and smaller down to the last one sitting right on the edge of the world. The bridges between look like bad stitching.

Been watching a thing without meaning to. The far spans are worse kept than ours. Every blow, the repair crews start on our bridges and work outward and never seem to reach the end of the line. Third season I've watched them not reach it. You'd think the company forgot it hung a rig out there at all.

Gulls left early again tonight. All at once, the way they go. Had the whole rail to myself after.

pump_room_tag.title: LAMINATED TAG — FLOODED PUMP ROOM
pump_room_tag.body:
PUMP ROOM 1-C — LOCKOUT / TAGOUT

DO NOT RESTART. Bilge pumps down for impeller service.
Dated the 11th. The month's a smear.

The wheel it's clipped to sits under water now. Whoever hung it meant to be back that same shift — the prybar's still on the bench where they set it down.

coffee_note.title: NAPKIN UNDER A FULL COFFEE CUP — GALLEY
coffee_note.body:
Pencil, quick hand, tucked under a mug gone cold:

'Osk — you covered my night, I owe you one. Fresh pot, made it at 0330. Drink it while it's hot.
Back in five.'

The mug is full. The pot is full. The stove underneath is stone cold.

roof_mark.title: CHALK TALLY — BUNKHOUSE ROOF
roof_mark.body:
Somebody spent hours up here. Chalk marks on the roof plate, weather-worn, grouped in fives — thirty-one of them. Then a stretch of nothing. Then four more, added later, pressed down so hard they scored the steel.

Beside the count, a chalk drawing: a flat line for the horizon, and above it a shape with wide flat wings. Under that, three words, gone over and over till the chalk snapped:

IT COMES BACK

shrine_note.title: KELP-WRAPPED NOTE — CABIN B-03
shrine_note.body:
they said burn the kelp off with the rest of it. i didn't.

it's not rot and it's not weed. hold a frond up in the dark and it keeps a light down inside it, low and steady, like a pilot flame that won't gutter out. i've had this one a week. hasn't dimmed once. a thing that meant you harm wouldn't burn that clean.

porthole's cracked a finger's width. if the light out there wants in, let it come and say so.

— O.

cabin_b05_scrawl.title: SCRAWL ON THE WALL — CABIN B-05
cabin_b05_scrawl.body:
Grease pencil, big letters, running uphill toward the ceiling:

COUNTED 41 AT MUSTER.
BOAT LEFT WITH 40.

WHO STAYED. WHO STAYED. WHO

toolpusher_log.title: TOOLPUSHER'S LOG — FINAL PAGE
toolpusher_log.body:
0400 — Hole's gone quiet. Not the good quiet. Thirty years I've drilled and I know the difference between a well that's resting and a well that's holding its breath. This one's holding its breath.

0430 — Rang Control, told them we're shutting in. Not one man on the floor argued it. First time in thirty years nobody argued a shut-in.

0605 — Company man wants my reason in writing. Here's my reason in writing: the water lit up under leg four, bright as noon from below, and every gauge on this deck fell to zero inside the same half-second. All of them at once. Pressure does not do that. I've no next line to give you.

—

medbay_note.title: SICK-BAY LEDGER
medbay_note.body:
Day 11 — Deckhand R. in again. Says the shine off the water 'stays behind his eyes' after night watch — his words — and won't let go. No fever. Pupils even, reactive. Sleeping badly. Gave him something he won't take.

Day 12 — Two more with it, near the same words. None of the three share a watch. None of them drink together that I know of.

Day 13 — Stood at the rail after rounds and looked at it a good while longer than I meant to. Logging that I looked. Logging that R. isn't lying.

(The rest of the ledger is swollen with seawater, ink run, nothing legible.)

comms_log.title: LAST TRANSMISSION LOG
comms_log.body:
TX 2241 — SALTLINE-4 to STANCHION: evacuation away, less one soul, one crew unaccounted. Sea state 4. Bloom state — no code fits it. Visual on the water: AWAKE. That's the word I'm putting in the log. AWAKE.

RX 2244 — STANCHION: 4, say again your last, you're unreadable.

TX 2251 — SALTLINE-4: disregard my last. Going dark.

(Nothing logged after. The dial's still sitting on the guard channel.)

generator_tag.title: GENERATOR FAULT TAG
generator_tag.body:
OUT OF SERVICE — DO NOT CRANK

Fuel's contaminated — biological, thick, wrong colour to it. Filters fouled with a green residue that holds a faint light after dark. Stripped and cleaned them twice. Both times green again by morning.

You want power, the topside flood circuit still takes a splice at Breaker 4-A. Finding the cable's your problem. It was mine too.

— maintenance

mooring_log.title: MOORING WATCH LOG — STATION SW
mooring_log.body:
WINDLASS 4-SW — WATCH LOG

12th, day: chain washed down, links 40 through 60 regreased, tension nominal. Quiet watch.

13th, night: tension spiked around 0300, came off it by 0340. Swell out of the SW, nothing on the surface. Logged it, didn't call it up — nobody thanks you for a three-in-the-morning call over a swell.

14th, 0250: chain's drawing tight and there's no sea running to pull it. Something's on it, down past the waterline where the lamp won't reach. Going down to the landing to have a look.

(No entries after. Grease gun's still clipped to the rail, cap off.)

fender_tag.title: INSPECTION TAG — BOAT LANDING
fender_tag.body:
FENDER PANEL 3 — QUARTERLY INSPECTION

Rubbing strips 60% worn, replace next rotation. Tire fenders serviceable. Landing rated for the boats.

Inspector's initials worn down to a smear of salt.
Stamped along the bottom in the company's blue ink: MERIDIAN DEEP ENERGY — SALTLINE PROJECT.
Next service was booked for the 15th.

rigger_handbook.title: RIGGER'S HANDBOOK
rigger_handbook.body:
RIGGER'S HANDBOOK — SHOP COPY
Chained to the bench. Grease-thumbed, corners soft.

HOW THE BENCH WORKS
Press E at the bench to open it. Lay parts from your pack onto
the top — the bench shows what they want to become and what's
still missing. When a recipe is complete, hold WORK (or Space)
to hammer it real. Partial layouts are safe; take parts back
anytime. Some things must be seared here too, not just built.

————————————————————————————————
RECIPES

■ THROWING HOOK
   Needs: 1× Rope Coil + 1× Prybar
   Work: ~2s at the bench
   A heaving line with teeth. Takes back what the gyre holds.
   — Rope from the crane deck; prybar from the pump room.

■ PLANK WALKWAY
   Needs: 2× Driftwood Plank
   Work: ~2s at the bench
   A lashed plank section. Bridges a gap, extends a deck.
   — Two sound planks make a path where there wasn't one.

■ LEAN-TO
   Needs: 1× Canvas Tarp + 2× Driftwood Plank
   Work: ~3s at the bench
   Canvas over a driftwood frame. A pocket of warmth anywhere on the rig.
   — The sea gives back wood and canvas. Make a roof of them.

■ BARRICADE
   Needs: 1× Driftwood Plank + 2× Scrap Metal
   Work: ~3s at the bench
   Scrap plate on a wood brace. Waist-high, storm-solid.
   — Plate the gyre coughs up still remembers being a wall.

■ BLOOM LAMP
   Needs: 2× Kelp Bundle + 1× Scrap Metal
   Work: ~3s at the bench
   Bloom-kelp sealed in a scrap housing. Cold teal light, no power needed — and what walks at night honors it.
   — Kelp glows for weeks in a sealed housing. The crew knew.

■ DROP NET
   Needs: 2× Rope Coil + 1× Driftwood Plank
   Work: ~3s at the bench
   A weighted mesh on a winch line. Lower it off an edge, let the sea walk in, haul.
   — Set it before dusk — the night shift swims shallower.

■ SEARED GLOW WORM
   Needs: 1× Glow Worm
   Work: ~2s at the bench
   A minute on hot steel and the light goes out of it. What's left is honest meat.
   — Raw ones bite back on the way down. Sear it first.

————————————————————————————————
FISHING (a later hand, in pencil)
Rod's in the storeroom. Cast to open water [LMB], strike when
the float plunges, then reel the lulls and rest the surges —
if the strain bar tops out, the line parts. The drop net does
the patient version: build it AT A DECK EDGE, lower, walk away,
haul. Raw catch sears on the galley stove upstairs. Eat cooked.

A last note, pencilled in the margin:
"The gyre keeps giving it back. Rope, plank, plate, canvas.
 Whatever you lose to the water washes up by the third dawn.
 Build like the sea's on your side. It is."

anglers_notes.title: ANGLER'S NOTES
anglers_notes.body:
ANGLER'S NOTES — WET DECK COPY
A rigger's log of what the water gives, and when. Kept honest.

READ THE WATER: every cast tells you the conditions — the hour,
rig shadow or open water, storm or calm, worklight on the swell.
Match the fish to the water and the water stops being luck.

■ COPPER SPRAT   (rod+net)
   When: dawn/day/dusk/night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: surface
   Bait-tier shoals that trail anything moving. The sea's small change.

■ LANTERN HERRING   (rod+net)
   When: dawn/day/dusk/night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: surface
   The gateway catch. At night the shoal glows its own position away.

■ SLATE COD   (rod+net)
   When: day · Water: anywhere · Weather: storms help · Depth: mid
   Loves a gray sky — bites double under storm cloud. Heavy, honest meat.

■ LODESTONE BREAM   (rod)
   When: day · Water: open water · Weather: any · Depth: deep
   Deep daylight water. Its magnetized bones spin a compass — catch enough, craft crude magnets, someday.

■ EMBER SNAPPER   (rod+net)
   When: day/dusk · Water: rig shadow · Weather: any · Depth: mid
   Warm-bodied — crowds the rig's outfalls and warm steel. Fish the shadow of the deck.

■ CHIMEFISH   (rod+net)
   When: dawn/day/dusk/night · Water: anywhere · Weather: calm only · Depth: mid
   Calm seas only — they won't ring in weather. Worth more traded than eaten, someday.

■ DRUM CROAKER   (rod+net)
   When: dawn/day/dusk/night · Water: anywhere · Weather: STORMS ONLY · Depth: mid
   Storm fish, full stop. You hear the chorus drumming through the hull as the rain comes — then they bite like they mean it.

■ MIRRORJACK   (rod)
   When: dawn/dusk · Water: open water · Weather: any · Depth: surface
   A dawn and dusk feeder in open water — fast, chrome, furious on the line.

■ SILVER LADDER   (rod)
   When: dawn · Water: open water · Weather: any · Depth: mid
   Dawn columns over open water — the shoal stacks vertical, a shimmering pillar.

■ BARREL GROUPER   (rod)
   When: dawn/day/dusk/night · Water: open water · Weather: storms help · Depth: deep
   Sears to a PRIME FILLET.
   The hardest fight on the rod. Deep open water; a storm stirs them up off the bottom. Feeds you for days.

■ SABLE HAKE   (rod+net)
   When: night · Water: rig shadow · Weather: any · Depth: mid
   Drawn to worklight — power the floodlights, fish the glow.
   Rises to worklight after dark like moths with fins. Power the floodlights and fish the glow.

■ INKWELL SQUID   (rod+net)
   When: night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: mid
   Drawn to worklight — power the floodlights, fish the glow.
   Night jigging. Comes up backwards in a huff of luminous ink — the ink's worth keeping too, someday.

■ THE LOOKER   (rod)
   When: night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: deep
   Never kept. You'll understand at the rail.
   Any water, any hour, almost never. It is not kept. You'll understand at the rail.

■ GHOST SOLE   (rod+net)
   When: night · Water: rig shadow · Weather: any · Depth: mid
   Drawn to worklight — power the floodlights, fish the glow.
   Near-invisible by day. Night water near a glow is where it shows itself.

■ GLASSPIKE   (rod)
   When: night · Water: open water · Weather: calm only · Depth: surface
   Clear still nights, open water — a pike you see through, found by the grit in its gut.

■ RIBBON EEL   (rod)
   When: night · Water: open water · Weather: any · Depth: deep
   Sears to a PRIME FILLET.
   Deep dark water only. Comes up faintly crackling — the Bloom keeps strange batteries.

■ GUTTER PRAWN   (net)
   When: dawn/day/dusk/night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: mid
   Net filler. A soak rarely comes up without a few — the pens will want them, someday.

■ MILLER'S FLOUNDER   (net)
   When: day · Water: rig shadow · Weather: any · Depth: deep
   Deck-plate camouflage, bottom habits. Nets working close to the legs find them by day.

■ STONE CRAB   (net)
   When: dusk/night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: deep
   Walks into a soaked net, never onto a hook. Shell's ceramic-hard — keep the pieces, someday.

■ FATHOM HALIBUT   (net)
   When: night · Water: anywhere · Weather: any · Depth: deep
   Sears to a PRIME FILLET.
   Door-sized. Only a night-soaked net brings one up, and the winch knows about it. Feeds a week.

————————————————————————————————
Margins, later hand: "The net gathers, the rod hunts. The stove
makes it a meal. Raw will turn on you — a minute on hot steel won't."

KEEPING IT: raw turns in ~4 hours. HANG it on a marked line (raw
→ rotten, cooked → DRIED, keeps forever) or STOW it in the galley
fridge (always fresh). The sea below the swell is swimmable now —
cold, patrolled, and past ~13m down, not yours. Dock ladder's the
way back up.

osk_watch_slate.title: Night Watch Slate
osk_watch_slate.body:
Grease pencil on a watch slate, half wiped for the next shift to write over.

0210 quiet. 0245 quiet. 0310 —

it isn't in the water. the water is in IT. i put the lamp on it and it didn't run and it didn't come at me either. it turned. slow. the way a man turns when someone back down the deck says his name.

Henrik reckons i spook easy. eleven years i've watched this water. tonight was the first night it was the water doing the watching, and it had been at it a while, i think, before i felt it.

— O.

osk_last_note.title: Folded Note, Weighted With a Shell
osk_last_note.body:
Whoever finds this — don't hold the boat for me. i'm not coming down to the boats.

it isn't sickness. it isn't the fear either, i'm the far side of that now. R. told the medic it stays behind your eyes. R. had it turned around. it doesn't stay behind your eyes. it stays in front of them, out on the water, and once you've watched the sea lit up from the inside you can't go back to wanting the dark.

i'm going the other way down the line. east, toward the light, while the rest of you row for a shore that quit answering. don't grieve it. i picked it.

keep the lamps lit. not for me — i won't want them where i'm headed. for whoever the machine gives back.

— Osk

sat_dive_log.title: Saturation Log — Laminated Card
sat_dive_log.body:
BELL RUN 14 — SAT DAY 09 OF 16
Diver at storage depth. DO NOT DECOMPRESS OFF SCHEDULE.

Under the printed lines, in pen, fast, a different hand:

'muster's been called and we can't bring you up in time — nine days of gas in your blood, the bell would kill you on the way up. so we're sealing you in the pod. it runs its own decompress, six days, slow and safe, whatever happens topside. i set it myself. checked it twice.
i'm sorry. God, i'm sorry to leave a man in a can. we'll leave a lamp burning on the rail for you.
don't be angry we went. be alive when it opens.'

chess_note.title: Score Card Under a Chess Piece
chess_note.body:
Werner's up 3 games to 2. The board's mid-game, white to move. A scrap of card wedged under the white king, blocky capitals, Kristjan's hand:

'WERNER. IF I'M NOT BACK BY THE TIME YOU READ THIS, WHITE MATES IN FOUR AND YOU KNOW FULL WELL IT DOES. DON'T YOU DARE SWEEP THE BOARD. LEAVE IT EXACTLY AS IT SITS. SOME OF US ARE COMING BACK TO WIN IT HONEST.
— K.'

White never moved.

raft_plan.title: Drafting-Table Sketch
raft_plan.body:
Through the shop glass, weighted flat under a wrench: a raft, drawn careful and to scale, the sums for the hull worked twice down the margin. Oil drums for buoyancy. Deck plate for a keel. A mast stepped off a length of derrick pipe. A stores list in the corner — and that's where the missing forty percent went, a tin at a time, into a locker built under the bench to hold it.

Later, across the whole sheet, in a hand gone shaky:
'no good. the sea turns everything back. Osk was right. there's no west any more. only down the line.'

The raft's three planks short of finished. The saw is still set in the last cut.

henrik_photo.title: Photograph Taped Inside a Bunk
henrik_photo.body:
Two boys on a grey stony beach, squinting into the sun, holding up a fish far too small to keep. On the back, in round careful handwriting:

'They caught it themselves. Told the whole school their father's a deep-sea man. Come home and be one on dry land a while. — M.'

Still taped to the bunk board. Whoever slept here cleared out everything else and left the photo. Three weeks, he kept writing in his letters home. Three weeks.

company_man_memo.title: Sealed Directive — Eyes Only
company_man_memo.body:
MERIDIAN DEEP ENERGY — PROJECT SALTLINE
RE: TERMINUS YIELD — CONTAINMENT POSTURE

Yield at Platform 7 now exceeds projection by an order of magnitude and no longer responds to the inhibitor feed. Cease all internal reference to it as a contaminant. It is the product. It was always the product.

Line crews are NOT to be advised. Panic depresses output. Hold the provisioning schedule as issued — the yield takes the organic input, and it must be kept feeding through quarter end.

Across the wax seal, in pencil, bearing down hard enough to tear the paper:
'the organic input was us. all of us. 900 miles out so nobody ashore would hear the line go quiet.'

ev_last_splice.title: Note Pinned to the Breaker Panel
ev_last_splice.body:
If you're reading this, you found the splice notes and you got the topside lights up. Good. Means there's someone in the rig again.

i couldn't get us cable. They took every last spool down the line, same as they took everything. So here's what i've got for you instead — the one thing a chief owes a stranger:

the crab won't cross a lit lamp. Not because it's frightened. Because it's got manners. Somebody down the line built the thing that way — taught something the size of a table to mind a light — and i've quit letting myself wonder what for.

Keep the lamps burning. That's the whole of the job now. That's all of it.

— E.V.

bottle_note.title: Note in a Bottle
bottle_note.body:
Salt-swollen paper, corked with candle wax. It came in against the dock the way everything comes in here — the current won't have it any other way.

no name on it, just a hand:

if you're reading this you're on a rig and you're alive, and that alone makes you rare now. we got the boats off Rig 6. the sea won't let them run west. every time we put the bow toward shore it turns us, slow, back toward the line. we've stopped fighting it. rowing back in. tell whoever's on 4 to put a lamp in a window.

three days out if the current's kind. it hasn't been unkind. it just won't let us leave.

ops_watch_log.title: WATCH LOG — OPERATIONS LOOKOUT
ops_watch_log.body:
TOPSIDE WATCH — RUNNING

0400 — Wind backing hard out of the NE, sea building under it. Glass falling quicker than the old man says he's ever watched it fall. Squall line stood up on the west horizon, walking our way.

0620 — Supply boat overdue thirty-one hours. No horn, no lights, no answer on 16. From up here I can see the whole length of the line and there's not one hull moving on it. Seven rigs, and the only thing crossing between them is weather.

1130 — Storm's on us. Can't make out the next platform through the rain. Lightning cracks and you get one white instant of all seven strung out east, then it's black again.

Different pen, bearing down hard, at the foot of the page:
'watch isn't for ships any more. watch the WATER. it lights up on the bad nights and it comes nearest on the bad nights. don't lean on the rail.'

radio_log.title: RADIO SET — LAST TRAFFIC
radio_log.body:
The set's still live, dial lit, needle resting on the field guard channel. A spiral pad beside it holds the last calls anyone stopped to write down.

'— any SALTLINE station, this is 7, we've lost the inhibitor feed, repeat, lost the feed, the yield's up in the moon pool and it will not —'

'— 6 to the line, boats won't answer the helm, the sea's turning us back, does anybody copy, the sea is TURN—'

'— control, control, this is 4 topside, who's receiving. anybody. we kept the lamps lit. we did every last thing the notes told us to. is there a west out there. please. is there still a west —'

The pad's blank after that. Somebody kept the set powered anyway — it's warm to the touch. The guard channel hisses, and every so often, under the hiss, there's a sound that doesn't belong to any weather.
